hints: Focus on what atomisation really means, forming one mole of separate gaseous atoms starting from the element itself.
Remember iodine is a solid in its normal standard state at room temperature, so you must start from $\text{I}_2(\text{s})$, not $\text{I}_2(\text{g})$.
Check the moles to make exactly one mole of $\text{I}(\text{g})$, so think about what fraction of $\text{I}_2$ you need.
walkthrough:
**Recall the definition of atomisation**

Standard enthalpy of atomisation is the enthalpy change when 1 mole of gaseous atoms is formed from the element in its standard state.

Key rule:
$$\text{element (standard state)} \rightarrow 1 \text{ mol of } \text{X(g)}$$

**Find the standard state of iodine**

Iodine is a dark grey solid at standard conditions ($298 \text{ K}$, $100 \text{ kPa}$), so the element side must be $\text{I}_2(\text{s})$.

This immediately rules out any equation starting with $\text{I}_2(\text{g})$.

**Fix the moles to make one gaseous atom**

We need exactly $1$ mol of $\text{I(g)}$. Since each $\text{I}_2$ gives two $\text{I}$ atoms, we need only half a mole of $\text{I}_2$.

Correct equation:
$$\frac{1}{2}\text{I}_2(\text{s}) \rightarrow \text{I(g)}$$

options.A: Starts from $\text{I}_2(\text{g})$, but the standard state of iodine is solid. This is actually the bond dissociation enthalpy of $\text{I}_2$ gas, not atomisation from the element.
options.B: Wrong on two counts. It starts from $\text{I}_2(\text{g})$ instead of $\text{I}_2(\text{s})$, and it makes $2$ mol of $\text{I(g)}$ instead of $1$ mol.
options.C: Perfect match. It starts from the standard state $\text{I}_2(\text{s})$ and produces exactly $1$ mol of gaseous atoms, $\text{I(g)}$. This is the definition of $\Delta H_{at}$ for iodine.
options.D: Starts correctly from $\text{I}_2(\text{s})$ but produces $2$ mol of $\text{I(g)}$. Atomisation must give only $1$ mol, so this value would be twice the atomisation enthalpy.
